topline.text: The OECD's Education at a Glance 2026, published yesterday, confirms England as one of the worst performers on teacher attrition — about 10% left the profession in the latest year, and over 90% of leavers quit voluntarily before retirement, the highest share of any comparator country.

A new statutory Information Sharing Duty comes into force today under the Children's Wellbeing and Schools Act 2026, requiring schools to proactively share safeguarding-relevant information with other agencies.
topline.action: Check your DSL knows the duty is live from today and has read the statutory guidance.

diary.text: Labour's conference closes in Liverpool; the new Information Sharing Duty statutory guidance takes effect for all schools and colleges.
NEU national executive reconvenes to decide whether to relaunch the paused strike ballot.

items.lede: England's teacher attrition rate laid bare in new OECD data.
items.body: Education at a Glance 2026, published yesterday, shows around 10% of England's teachers left the profession in the latest year measured — over three times the rate in France or Ireland — and more than 90% of those leavers quit voluntarily before retirement, the highest such share in the comparison group. Separate OECD figures show English primary teachers' real-terms pay fell 3.6% between 2015 and 2024.
items.action: Useful external context for SLT/governors if retention comes up in exit interviews or a staff survey this term.

items.lede: Information Sharing Duty statutory guidance takes effect today.
items.body: Under the Children's Wellbeing and Schools Act 2026, schools and colleges now have a proactive legal duty to share information relevant to a child's safeguarding or welfare with other agencies, unless sharing would be more harmful than staying silent — aimed at removing the 'better not to share' reflex inquiries have repeatedly flagged.
items.action: Make sure your DSL has read the guidance and it's referenced in your child protection policy before the next review.

sections.heading: Sheffield: the odds of a successful appeal

items.lede: Nearly 1 in 3 Sheffield secondary appeals succeeded this year — but the rate is falling.
items.body: Of 358 Sheffield households who appealed a Year 7 place for September 2026, 73 succeeded — a 29.3% success rate, down from 35.3% the year before and well below high-success outliers like Sunderland (88.4%). Figures reported via The Star from official DfE admission appeals statistics.
items.action: If you support families through admissions, the falling success rate is worth flagging — a strong, well-evidenced first preference matters more this year.

box.label: Jargon-buster - Information Sharing Duty
box.intro: New from today under the Children's Wellbeing and Schools Act 2026.
box.text: A proactive legal duty on schools and named agencies to share safeguarding-relevant information with each other, rather than only responding to requests — unless sharing would cause more harm than staying silent.
